npcs.name: Kamal, lost property clerk at Fennell Street

nodes.line: Umbrellas. Nine hundred umbrellas. And one thing off the Fennell Street line that has a name on it and a phone number that rings out.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: I cannot leave the counter. You can. Go to the address on the tag and see who is not answering.
People come back for the strangest things. Nobody ever comes back for an umbrella.
That explains the phone. Poor sod. Put it back in the room, would you.

npcs.name: Kamila, commuter of long standing at Hawthorne

nodes.line: The quiet carriage works because everyone agrees it works. That is the whole mechanism. There is no other mechanism.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Speakerphone. Every morning, Hawthorne to town, speakerphone. I have made eye contact eleven times and it has done nothing.
I could move carriages. I have thought about it. But then they have won something.
Quiet. Genuinely quiet. I had forgotten what it sounded like.

npcs.name: Kaori, courier at North Strathfield

nodes.line: Forty drops a day. The difference between the shortcut and the long way at North Strathfield is nine minutes, and nine minutes is four drops.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Go and look at the lock. Tell me if it is a padlock or a decision.
A padlock I can live with. A decision I have to reroute around for the rest of my life.
A decision. Right. Nine minutes, forever. That is what that is.

npcs.name: Kareem, trackwork foreman at Taverners Hill

nodes.line: Midnight to four, Taverners Hill is mine. Nobody thanks you for it and nobody sees it and by six it looks like nothing happened.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Somebody is walking through. Not kids. Kids run. This one walks.
You do not get a second warning out here. You get a grinder and a very long report.
Good. Now I can fill in a form and somebody else can ignore it.

npcs.name: Karina, publican at Stanmore

nodes.line: Nineteen years. Same stool. Then nothing, and every regular in this bar has gone vague on me at once, which means they know.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Go and knock. You have got a face nobody here owes anything to.
I have kept the stool. That is either respect or superstition, I have stopped being able to tell.
Ah. Well. I will keep the stool anyway.

npcs.name: Kasia, commuter car park attendant at Koolewong

nodes.line: Two hundred bays at Koolewong. I have counted two hundred and forty cars in here on a Tuesday. Do that arithmetic.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Bay 14 has not moved since March. Photograph it. I want a date somebody can be embarrassed by.
You cannot tow it without an owner and you cannot find an owner without towing it. That is the whole job.
March. In writing. Now it is somebody else's March.

npcs.name: Kata, council contractor at Normanhurst

nodes.line: Grey. I have one colour and it is grey and it is the same grey in every suburb in this city.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: There is one near Normanhurst that I am scheduled to kill on Thursday. I would like something of it to exist afterwards.
I keep the photos. Two hundred and eleven of them. It is the worst gallery in Australia.
Two hundred and twelve. Right. Thursday can have the wall.

npcs.name: Kaveh, bus driver on a break at Beecroft

nodes.line: Eleven times a shift past Beecroft and up over that hill. Six years. Never stopped.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: I am not going to stop. That is not the kind of person I turned out to be. So you go.
There is a bench up there. I have watched it from a moving bus about fourteen thousand times.
That is what it looks like. Right. That is what it looks like.

npcs.name: Kayo, someone with a grievance at Gymea

nodes.line: Two hundred and eighty-five dollars. Gymea. For a thing the sign did not say, because the sign is not there.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: The form wants evidence. How do you photograph a thing not being somewhere? That is your problem now.
It is not the money. It is that the form has a box for it and the box assumes I am lying.
Perfect. Absence, photographed. Let them argue with that.

npcs.name: Keanu, guerrilla gardener at Parramatta Square

nodes.line: A metre of dirt at Parramatta Square. Eleven years of nothing and cigarette ends.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Council mows it on the fifteenth. Council does not know what is in it. I would like the fifteenth to go badly for council.
Nobody planted it. I planted it. Nobody is going to know that and that is the point of it.
It survived. Good. Next year it will be twice that and they will assume it was always there.

npcs.name: Keiko, night-fill supervisor at Green Square

nodes.line: Ten to six. Six of us, forty aisles, one radio that only gets the one station.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Somebody knows our roster. They come in off the late train at Green Square and they are gone before the first delivery.
I have worked nights eight years. You stop being able to tell whether you are tired or just awake at the wrong time.
Knew our roster. Of course they did. Nothing in this job is ever a stranger.

npcs.name: Kelvin, first-floor tenant at Wahroonga

nodes.line: Nine years above Wahroonga. I do not hear the trains any more, which means I hear it instantly when one of them is wrong.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: A month ago the rhythm changed. Same trains, different sound. Go and find out what they did to my track.
Everyone says you get used to it. You do. That is the frightening part.
Thank you. Nine years and the first person who went and listened.

npcs.name: Kenji, stallholder at Lisarow

nodes.line: Five in the morning at Lisarow, in the dark, unloading a van by feel.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: He is coming at four now. Four. There is no rule about four because nobody thought a person would do that.
Twenty-six years in this market. The bays are not allocated. They are just known.
Known again. Good. You cannot write it down, that is the trouble with it.

npcs.name: Keziah, station master at Martin Place

nodes.line: Four minutes fast. Every relief who comes through Martin Place wants to be the one who fixes it.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Somebody set it that way on purpose and everybody who knows why is nearly gone. Find out before they are.
Half this network runs on things somebody decided in 1974 and never wrote down.
Right. Then it stays four minutes fast, and now two of us know why.

npcs.name: Khadija, someone at the end of their patience at Yallamundi

nodes.line: Every weekday. The 5:40 into Yallamundi. Sits at the yellow line and waits and then walks off on its own.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: I am not doing another winter of watching that. Find out where it goes and who it belongs to.
Half the platform knows. Nobody has done anything, including me, for four months.
Not a sad story. I will take it. I badly needed one that was not.

npcs.name: Khalil, bookmaker of the informal kind at Canley Vale

nodes.line: Nothing illegal. A book on small things. Weather, delays, whether the 7:02 out of Canley Vale is on time.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Somebody is up four hundred over eleven weeks on the delay market. That is not luck, that is information.
You cannot beat a delay book unless you can see the roster. Think about who can see the roster.
The roster. I am not even angry. I am going to hire them.

npcs.name: Kiara, night guard at Erskineville

nodes.line: You get to know the last service. Four people out of Erskineville and one of them is asleep every single night, and it is never the same one.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Ride it to Macdonaldtown. Photograph the platform with nobody on it. I want to know the place exists when I am not standing in it.
Twenty-two years. I have watched this place empty out twenty-two years and I still do not like the sound it makes.
There it is. Still there. Good. Some nights I am not sure.

npcs.name: Kieran, ticket inspector at Wolli Creek

nodes.line: Card ending 70. Taps on at Wolli Creek, six-forty, every weekday. Never taps off. Not once in four months.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: I am not allowed to follow it and you are not employed, which makes you better at this than me. Find where they get off.
It is not the money. It is ninety cents a day. It is that I cannot work out how.
A hole in a fence. Four months. I want to be angry and mostly I am impressed.

npcs.name: Kiri, kiosk operator at Thirroul

nodes.line: Two hundred a morning through Thirroul. I know them by the walk before I know them by the face.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: One of them stopped. Three weeks. Take one over there and find out if I lost them to the chain up the road.
If it is the chain I would rather they were dead. I am joking. Mostly.
The chain. Of course it was the chain. Thank you for finding out. I hate it.

npcs.name: Kirra, relief signaller at Richmond

nodes.line: Four minutes. That board has said four minutes since before the merge. Sometimes it means four minutes.

choices.text: How long have you been at this?

nodes.line: Nobody upstairs believes me because I have no data, only twelve years. Go and get me data.
A minute of a stranger's life, three hundred times a day. Somebody should write it down.
Right. Now I have a number, and a number is a thing they have to answer.
